questions.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\,x{y}^{2}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\,dx+x{y}^{2}\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/0cb340ef33d4cc38081e3796b4c8e076f1499760c0a3ffeecb8123a41fefeec8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y+{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\,dx+x{y}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({y}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}-1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta -r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨xy-\sqrt[3]{x+5},\,x+2y⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(xy-\sqrt[3]{x+5})\,dx+(x+2y)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/798665574b8f0e11d991bb0d934efd01bdeb65840c2e86498be4edbc59578439.png)

Since $P(x,y)=xy-\sqrt[3]{x+5}$ and $Q(x,y)=x+2y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(xy-\sqrt[3]{x+5})\,dx+(x+2y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}r-{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨x{y}^{2},\,x+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡y}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+(x+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡y})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/d831c7fb805d16ec7a2dc2462813ea79b78d888ed2121330ed5d823b590d3c4f.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x{y}^{2}\,dx+(x+{e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2xy)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2xy)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}r-{r}^{3}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}r-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-{x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-2xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx-{x}^{2}y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 5,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-2xy-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2\cdot r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(-2{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{5}-{r}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{3}\,dx-{x}^{3}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/8cb15d895d5baf46d359d811fce99b73238434eb01079d1199cfd99d3f52f222.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨{y}^{2}+{x}^{2},\,xy+y{e}^{y}⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,dx+(xy+y{e}^{y})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/232ced663dcac27ce2775af66dd2ef215ed937e0f4eb5e3e6fb008a3d82dc069.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}+{x}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=xy+y{e}^{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+{x}^{2})\,dx+(xy+y{e}^{y})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,-\pi \le \theta \le 0\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{0}\,{\int }_{0}^{1}-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Given that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/1e78bf74df5607a1d80b3bd51b3222505e3bb201817448a7a5ebe5b0a73cffa9.svg)
where $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = \left\langle y^2+\sin x, \: 3xy-\cos y  \right\rangle$ and $C$ is the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (y^2+\sin x) \: \mathrm{d}x + (3xy-\cos y) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/798665574b8f0e11d991bb0d934efd01bdeb65840c2e86498be4edbc59578439.png)

Since $P(x,y)= y^2+\sin x$ and $Q(x,y)= 3xy-\cos y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,dx+(xy-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0\leq r \leq 2,\: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi  \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, the missing expression is $r^2\sin\theta.$

Find a repeated integral in plane polar coordinates that's equivalent to $\displaystyle \oint\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathrm{d}\mathbf{r} \, .$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\mathbf{F}\cdot\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}
=
\oint\limits_{C} (2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left( e^{y/3} + 3x \right) \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/e4c7913793a4b08916a832e575c5b2c167d5dfeec244eea23857731df1e514e7.png)

Since $P(x,y)= 2y + \ln{(\sqrt{x+5})}$ and $Q(x,y)=e^{y/3} + 3x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2y+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x+5}))\,dx+({e}^{y/3}+3x)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
\Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \right\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{3}r\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to evaluate the line integral

$$
\oint\limits_{C}\left( e^{-x^2}- x^2y \right) \: \mathrm{d}x + \left(y+xy^2\right) \mathrm{d}y,
$$

where $C$ is the unit circle $x^2 + y^2 = 1,$ oriented counterclockwise. 

Direct evaluation of this integral is likely to be a difficult task. However, we can make light work of this tricky integral using Green's theorem.

Recall that Green's theorem states the following:

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ (shown below) satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223987/assets/dd859c753a8a5445eafab5db4f1e796b48997e1abb1728accd03fe3825e595d6.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y) = e^{-x^2}- x^2y, \qquad Q(x,y) = y+xy^2,
$$

we obtain the partial derivatives   

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{-{x}^{2}}-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(y+x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

This double integral will be easier to evaluate if we switch to plane polar coordinates. 

The region $D$ in $xy$-coordinates can be represented as the region $\Delta$ in polar coordinates, given by

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: 0 \leq \theta \leq 2\pi \big\}.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
\iint\limits_{D} f(x,y) \ \mathrm d A = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r \cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \:  r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta.
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral by applying the change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\pi \cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$
